title: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta
text: There are these four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; union with what is displeasing is suffering; separation from what is pleasing is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering. This suffering has a cause: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for extermination. This suffering can cease through the cessation of craving. The path leading to the cessation of suffering is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

title: Satipatthana Sutta
text: There is one way for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for reaching the right path, for the realization of Nibbana: the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Contemplation of the body, contemplation of feelings, contemplation of mind, contemplation of mental objects. A practitioner abides contemplating the body as body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. The same applies to feelings, mind, and mental objects.

title: Anattalakkhana Sutta
text: Form is not-self. If form were self, it would not lead to affliction. Feeling is not-self. Perception is not-self. Mental formations are not-self. Consciousness is not-self. What do you think: Is form permanent or impermanent? Impermanent. Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? Suffering. Is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? No. Therefore, any form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—should be seen as it actually is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'

title: Saccavibhanga Sutta
text: The truth of suffering should be understood. The truth of the origin of suffering should be abandoned. The truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized. The truth of the path should be developed. What is suffering? Birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering. Association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what is wanted is suffering. The origin of suffering is craving: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for being, craving for non-being. The cessation of suffering is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving. The path to the cessation of suffering is this Noble Eightfold Path.

title: Paticca-samuppada-vibhanga Sutta
text: With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises. With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise. With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise. With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises. With contact as condition, feeling arises. With feeling as condition, craving arises. With craving as condition, clinging arises. With clinging as condition, becoming arises. With becoming as condition, birth arises. With birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. Through the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations, and so on, leading to the cessation of the entire mass of suffering.

title: Anapanasati Sutta
text: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and benefit. One sits down, having folded the legs crosswise, sets the body erect, and establishes mindfulness in front. Breathing in long, one understands 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, one understands 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, one understands 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, one understands 'I breathe out short.' One trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body. I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' One trains thus: 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation. I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation.' In this way, mindfulness of breathing fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of enlightenment, and true knowledge and liberation.

title: Sammaditthi Sutta
text: Right view is understanding the unwholesome and the wholesome, understanding the four nutriments, understanding the Four Noble Truths, understanding aging and death. When one knows and sees the eye as impermanent, one knows and sees the truth. When one knows and sees forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as impermanent, one knows and sees the truth. When one understands suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, one has right view.

title: Mulapariyaya Sutta
text: An untaught ordinary person perceives earth as earth. Having perceived earth as earth, they conceive themselves as earth, they conceive themselves in earth, they conceive themselves apart from earth, they conceive earth to be 'mine,' they delight in earth. The same applies to water, fire, air, beings, gods, and Nibbana. But one who has destroyed the taints does not conceive, does not delight, having understood as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these phenomena.

title: Kalama Sutta
text: Do not go upon what has been acquired by repeated hearing, nor upon tradition, nor upon rumor, nor upon scripture, nor upon surmise, nor upon axiom, nor upon specious reasoning, nor upon bias towards a notion pondered over, nor upon another's seeming ability, nor upon the consideration 'The monk is our teacher.' When you yourselves know: 'These things are unwholesome, these things are blameworthy, these things are censured by the wise, these things, when undertaken and observed, lead to harm and suffering,' then you should abandon them. And when you yourselves know: 'These things are wholesome, these things are blameless, these things are praised by the wise, these things, when undertaken and observed, lead to welfare and happiness,' then you should enter and remain in them.

title: Maharahulovada Sutta
text: Develop meditation on loving-kindness, for when you develop loving-kindness, ill will will be abandoned. Develop meditation on compassion, for when you develop compassion, cruelty will be abandoned. Develop meditation on appreciative joy, for when you develop appreciative joy, aversion will be abandoned. Develop meditation on equanimity, for when you develop equanimity, irritation will be abandoned. Develop meditation on the foul, for when you develop meditation on the foul, lust will be abandoned. Develop meditation on the perception of impermanence, for when you develop the perception of impermanence, the conceit 'I am' will be abandoned.

title: Sabbasava Sutta
text: There are taints to be abandoned by seeing, by restraining, by using, by enduring, by avoiding, by removing, and by developing. Some taints should be abandoned by seeing with wisdom. Some should be abandoned by restraining the sense faculties. Some should be abandoned by proper use of requisites. Some should be abandoned by enduring cold, heat, hunger, and thirst. Some should be abandoned by avoiding dangerous animals, rough places, and bad companions. Some should be abandoned by removing unwholesome thoughts. Some should be abandoned by developing the seven factors of enlightenment. When a practitioner has abandoned taints by these seven methods, they are called one who has cut off craving, removed the fetters, and made an end of suffering.

title: Mahasatipatthana Sutta
text: In this teaching, a practitioner goes to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, and establishes mindfulness in front of them. Mindful, they breathe in; mindful, they breathe out. They know when breathing in long, when breathing out long, when breathing in short, when breathing out short. They contemplate the body in the body, feelings in feelings, mind in mind, and phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.

title: Ādittapariyāya Sutta
text: All is burning. And what is the all that is burning? The eye is burning, forms are burning, eye-consciousness is burning, eye-contact is burning. The ear is burning, sounds are burning. The nose is burning, odors are burning. The tongue is burning, flavors are burning. The body is burning, tangibles are burning. The mind is burning, mental phenomena are burning. Burning with what? Burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. Burning with birth, aging, and death; with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Seeing thus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with eye-consciousness. Becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated.

title: Culamalunkya Sutta
text: It is as if a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison, and his friends brought a surgeon to treat him. The man would say: 'I will not let the surgeon pull out this arrow until I know the name and clan of the man who wounded me, whether he was tall or short, whether he was dark or light-skinned, whether he came from such a village or town.' That man would die without ever learning these things. In the same way, one who says 'I will not live the holy life under the Blessed One until he explains to me whether the world is eternal or not eternal, whether the world is finite or infinite'—that person would die before the Tathagata ever explained this. The holy life does not depend on these views. What I have explained is suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path. Why? Because this is beneficial, this is the beginning of the holy life, and this leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbana.

title: Dasadhamma Sutta
text: Ten qualities should be reflected upon again and again by one who has gone forth: I am now changed into a different mode of life. My life depends on others. I should behave in a different way. Can I blame myself regarding my virtue? Could wise companions who investigate blame me regarding my virtue? I must be separated and parted from all that is dear and appealing to me. I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, and have my actions as my refuge; whatever I do, for good or for evil, to that will I fall heir. Day and night I should reflect on what I am doing with my life.

title: Bojjhanga-ahara Sutta
text: There is proper attention to things that are the basis for the arising of the enlightenment factors: mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. When you attend properly to things wholesome and unwholesome, to things blameworthy and blameless, to things inferior and superior, to things dark and bright, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena arises. When energy is aroused, the enlightenment factor of energy arises. When energy is aroused, spiritual joy arises. When the mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one feels pleasure. When one feels pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated. This is how the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated.

title: Sammaditthi Sutta
text: There are four distortions of perception, thought, and view: regarding the impermanent as permanent, regarding suffering as pleasure, regarding what is non-self as self, and regarding the foul as beautiful. There are four non-distortions: regarding the impermanent as impermanent, regarding suffering as suffering, regarding what is non-self as non-self, and regarding the foul as foul. For a long time this perception 'permanent' in regard to the impermanent has resided in your minds. That is how you have come under the sway of Mara. For a long time this perception 'pleasure' in regard to suffering has resided in your minds. For a long time this perception 'self' in regard to non-self has resided in your minds. For a long time this perception 'beautiful' in regard to the foul has resided in your minds.

title: Kakacūpama Sutta
text: Even if bandits were to sever you savagely limb by limb with a two-handled saw, one who gave rise to a mind of hate towards them would not be carrying out my teaching. You should train thus: 'Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no evil words; we shall abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate. We shall abide pervading them with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and starting with them, we shall abide pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.' That is how you should train.

title: Phena Sutta
text: Form is like a lump of foam. Feeling is like a bubble. Perception is like a mirage. Mental formations are like a plantain trunk. Consciousness is like a magic trick. However one may examine and investigate form, it will appear empty, hollow, and without substance. What substance could there be in a lump of foam? The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus the wise person contemplates these aggregates and sees them as empty, hollow, without substance. When one contemplates the aggregates thus, one abandons ignorance and clear knowledge arises. When ignorance is abandoned and clear knowledge has arisen, one is called one who truly sees.

title: Sankhitta Sutta
text: A practitioner is virtuous; they dwell restrained with the restraint of the monastic code, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults. Having undertaken the training rules, they train in them. They have heard much, remember what they have heard, and consolidate what they have heard. They have good friends, good companions, good comrades. They have energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and for acquiring wholesome qualities; they are steadfast, solid in their effort. They are wise; they possess wisdom directed to arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering.

title: Themes Sutta
text: Five themes should be often reflected upon by one who has gone forth: I am subject to aging, I have not gone beyond aging. I am subject to illness, I have not gone beyond illness. I am subject to death, I have not gone beyond death. I will grow different, separate from all that is dear and appealing to me. I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, and have my actions as my refuge. Whatever I do, for good or for evil, to that will I fall heir. These themes should be reflected upon often by all people, whether they have gone forth or not.

title: Sallekha Sutta
text: Though others may be harmful, we shall be harmless. Though others may kill living beings, we shall abstain from killing. Though others may take what is not given, we shall abstain from taking what is not given. Though others may be unchaste, we shall be chaste. Though others may speak falsely, we shall abstain from false speech. Though others may speak maliciously, divisively, harshly, or engage in idle chatter, we shall abstain from such speech. Though others may be covetous, we shall be without covetousness. Though others may have ill will, we shall be without ill will. Though others may have wrong view, we shall have right view. This is how effacement is practiced.

title: Yuganaddha Sutta
text: There are four ways of practice: painful practice with slow insight, painful practice with quick insight, pleasant practice with slow insight, and pleasant practice with quick insight. What is painful practice with slow insight? One dwells contemplating the body as unpleasant, full of repulsiveness, and their faculties are dull—this is painful practice with slow insight. What is pleasant practice with quick insight? One dwells secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhana with rapture and pleasure, and their faculties are sharp—this is pleasant practice with quick insight. Of these four, pleasant practice with quick insight is the foremost.

title: Sallatha Sutta
text: When the uninstructed worldling is contacted by a painful feeling, they sorrow, grieve, and lament; they weep beating their breast and become distraught. They feel two kinds of feelings: a bodily one and a mental one. It is as if a man were pierced by a dart, and then pierced by a second dart, so they feel the feelings of two darts. But when the instructed noble disciple is contacted by a painful feeling, they do not sorrow, grieve, or lament; they do not weep beating their breast or become distraught. They feel one kind of feeling: a bodily one, not a mental one. It is as if a man were pierced by a dart, but not pierced by a second dart, so they feel the feeling of only one dart.

title: Titthayatana Sutta
text: There are sectarians who hold this doctrine and view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.' There are sectarians who hold: 'Whatever this person experiences is caused by a supreme being's act of creation.' And there are sectarians who hold: 'Whatever this person experiences has no cause and no condition.' To those who say all is caused by past action, I ask: 'Then are not killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and all evil actions also caused by what was done in the past?' Thus this view has no reasonable basis. The Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,' and so forth.
